drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. A retail chain's head of operations has just watched your prototype
drills.answer_line: SAM: Because a sponsor hears any verdict as a commitment
drills.scenario: Retail sponsor wants a go-live date
drills.stem: A delighted head of operations asks you to commit today to a six-week build and a go-live date. You do not yet know daily contract volume, the longest input size, or the latency requirement. What is the best next action?

options.A: Commit to six weeks to keep momentum, refine scope in the first sprint
options.B: Issue a provisional feasibility verdict from the prototype, clearly labelled provisional
options.C: Gather volume, input size range and latency first, then give a verdict and write boundaries into the SOW
options.D: Propose the largest model tier for headroom on whatever volume turns up

drills.why: A sponsor hears any verdict as a commitment. Volume, input size and latency are inputs to the verdict; the prototype only answered the capability question.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A public-sector benefits agency briefs you. The requirements
drills.stem: Your drafted requirements for a benefits agency say documents are retained for 12 months, but nobody mentioned retention. What is the best next action?

options.A: Delete the retention item, since it was not requested
options.B: Keep it, because 12 months is standard practice
options.C: Label it an assumption, assign an owner, and ask the agency's compliance lead
options.D: Leave it in and let the legal review catch any problem

drills.why: Retention is a must-prove constraint. An assumption that traces to no statement is the most dangerous kind: label it, give it an owner, and ask.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A bank's chief operating officer must approve keeping
drills.stem: A bank COO must approve keeping long policy documents in full context rather than building retrieval. Your draft covers the simpler design and the per-call cost. Which two additions most improve the chance of an informed decision?

options.A: Projected monthly cost at forecast production volume, with caching evaluated
options.B: Cost of moving to retrieval after the system is built around full context
options.C: Detailed explanation of chunk sizes and embedding choices
options.D: Recommend deferring the decision until after launch
options.E: The p99 latency distribution from the prototype

drills.why: A turns a per-call rate into the number the executive owns. B is the reversal cost, the missing third element of a tradeoff.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A field-service company's repair-guidance assistant has seen
drills.answer_line: SAM: Yes. D. The signal already exists; the decision layer is missing
drills.scenario: Repair assistant, four weeks of drift
drills.stem: A repair-guidance assistant's eval score has fallen for four straight weeks. Error rate is flat, no alert has fired, and a regional manager says answers feel weaker. What is the best next action?

options.A: Add more dashboards so the drift is easier to see
options.B: Raise it at the next scheduled quarterly review
options.C: Move to a larger model tier
options.D: Diagnose prompt, data or model drift, add a quality-drift trigger with an owner, escalate once confirmed

drills.why: The signal already exists; the decision layer is missing. Fix the loop and the cause. B is how this pattern burns seven weeks.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Four weeks after launch, the sponsor of a claims-triage assistant
drills.stem: Four weeks after launch, a claims-triage sponsor wants the outcome document today for a CFO expansion meeting. Baseline processing time was measured before launch. What is the best next action?

options.A: Send volume, latency and error-rate figures now
options.B: Extrapolate the after metric from the first week's data
options.C: Name the measurement owner, confirm the authorisation log records, schedule completion at a set milestone
options.D: Tell the sponsor outcome reporting waits for the quarterly review

drills.why: The gate is not yet satisfied: the after metric needs runtime. A answers "does it run", B asserts a number without data, D withholds expectation-setting.

drills.question_line: SAM: Your turn first. Pause and name the five task statements we covered, and the artefact each one leaves behind. [pause]
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Discovery leaves a translation table. Tradeoffs leave a decision package.
drills.prompt: Name the five task statements we covered, and the artefact each one leaves behind.
drills.answer: Discovery: translation table. Tradeoffs: decision package. Feedback loops and SLAs: governance table. Documentation: decision log and control register. Lifecycle: an artefact gating each transition.

In this episode: Turn a vague word into a testable constraint
Spot the unknowns that block a feasibility verdict
Present a tradeoff with its reversal cost
Feedback loops and SLAs that decide, not display
Documentation a successor can act on
The artefact that gates each lifecycle phase
Cold open: the go-live date: 14%, about 9 items; the right answer removes risk at the root
Experience words like seamless are signals, not requirements
4 buckets: must do, must not do, must cost, must prove
Translation table: statement, constraint, decision forced, assumption
A prototype answers only the capability question
Communicating tradeoffs: Every tradeoff: gain, give-up, reversal cost; compliance posture if regulated
Reversal cost is the one dropped, and dropping it causes false alignment
Lead with the business outcome; cut technical depth, never cost
Executives: monthly cost at forecast volume, plus reversal cost
Security and legal: evidence, not assertions
Engineers: rejected alternatives and the tradeoff each resolved
Feedback loops and SLAs: Loop: signals, triage, decide, act, review
Governance table: each signal to a trigger, an owner and an action
Slow drift never fires a hard alert
SLA: what is measured, what counts as a breach, what happens next
Thresholds trace to UX expectation, criticality or eval criteria
Cost breaks first: production runs 1-2 orders of magnitude above pilot
Documentation for handoff: 3 readers: inheriting engineer, auditor, returning architect
Fields: dated decision, rejected alternatives, tradeoff, owner, evidence
Test: can someone not in the room make a safe change?
Record rejected alternatives when the decision is made
A diagram feels authoritative but is not proof
Outcome document: before-and-after on the business metric
Supporting the lifecycle: Phases: discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration
Gates: translation table, feasibility verdict, decision log and control register
Set regions explicitly on Bedrock or Vertex
Demo and go-to-market material: partner track, not tested
Go-live verdict: gather volume, input size and latency first
Any verdict before the missing constraints, provisional or not, is the trap
Five to remember: Seamless or fast signals more questions: translate to a testable constraint, label assumptions
Tradeoffs carry gain, give-up and reversal cost; dropping reversal cost causes false alignment
Monitoring is not a feedback loop: signal to trigger, owner, action; slow drift; scheduled checks
SLA thresholds trace to something real; forecast cost at production volume before the first invoice
Document decision, rejected alternatives, tradeoff; evidence for reviewers, before-and-after for sponsors
Recap: the exam tells: Seamless, fast or intuitive: a signal to ask more questions, not a requirement
Stem lists unknowns (volume, input size, latency): gather them before any verdict
Nobody mentioned it: label it an assumption, give it an owner, ask
Executive surprised by the invoice: missing reversal cost and monthly figure, false alignment
Score drifts for weeks, no alert: missing decision layer; diagnose, add a drift trigger with an owner
Successor broke a rule the design avoided: rejected alternatives never written down
Outcome document wanted too early: name the measurement owner, confirm logging, set the milestone
